The original measurements were taken using only a tape measure on disarticulated remains, leading to gross exaggerations. (IFLScience; Hale Tom; 2024)

20th Century Fox and New Regency Productions publicly acknowledged creating fake news websites to promote the film. They initially defended the campaign stating: "A Cure for Wellness is a movie about a 'fake' cure that makes people sicker... a 'fake' health and wellness website was created, healthandwellness.co, and we partnered with a fake news creator to publish fake news" (The New York Times; Stack Liam; 2017). Fox later issued an official apology: "The digital campaign was inappropriate under every point of view... In this case, we were wrong". (BuzzFeed News; Griffin Tamerra; 2017)

Fox utilized at least five fake websites designed to mimic local news outlets: The Sacramento Dispatch, Salt Lake City Guardian, Houston Leader, NY Morning Post, and Indianapolis Gazette. These sites shared similar designs, the same Google Analytics ID, and domain names registered on the same days (BuzzFeed News; Silverman, Lytvynenko; 2017). Additionally, they created thematic sites such as a fraudulent HealthCare.gov clone (HealthCureGov.com, registered to 20th Century Fox) and a fake bottled water company called Vita Acqua, claiming to source from a non-existent Swiss village. (The New York Times; Stack Liam; 2017)

The fabricated stories included sensational headlines such as "BOMBSHELL: Trump and Putin spotted at Swiss resort prior to election," "Trump Signs Executive Order Issuing 90-Day Ban on Childhood Vaccinations" (published on The Houston Leader and debunked by Snopes), and "'Trump Depression Disorder' Classified As A Disease By The American Medical Association," which urged readers to tweet #cureforwellness (The New York Times; Stack Liam; 2017). Another hoax about Lady Gaga planning a Muslim tribute during her Super Bowl performance generated over 50,000 Facebook shares (BuzzFeed News; Silverman, Lytvynenko; 2017). The sites also exploited real disasters, such as the Oroville dam crisis in California, falsely reporting that Trump had denied federal aid, generating over 20,000 interactions and anger against the president. (BuzzFeed News; Silverman, Lytvynenko; 2017)

The campaign was designed as viral marketing exploiting the 2017 political and media climate. The filmmakers initially defended the strategy as consistent with the film's plot, but the meta-narrative connection was obscure to the vast majority of readers, who shared the stories believing them to be real (The New York Times; Stack Liam; 2017). Ads on the fake sites directed readers to the film's official website. (BuzzFeed News; Griffin Tamerra; 2017)

The campaign caused significant collateral damage: in at least one case, a real local news outlet received a barrage of protest calls and emails due to confusion with the fake site (BuzzFeed News; Griffin Tamerra; 2017). Bonnie Patten, executive director of TruthinAdvertising.org, called the tactic "a form of deceptive marketing" that "absolutely crosses the line" (The New York Times; Stack Liam; 2017). Lynn Walsh, president of the Society of Professional Journalists, criticized the lack of labels clearly indicating the non-factual nature of the content (The New York Times; Stack Liam; 2017). After discovery, most fake domains were redirected to the film's official website. (BuzzFeed News; Silverman, Lytvynenko; 2017)

Between 2013 and 2020, Matrix LLC, a political consulting firm acting for Alabama Power and Florida Power & Light, channeled at least $900,000 to six news outlets in Alabama and Florida. Internal records reveal that Alabama Political Reporter (APR) received monthly payments of $8,000 starting in 2013, while Alabama Today received over $140,000. These financial ties were not disclosed to the public, and the outlets functioned as "pay-to-play" platforms for the utility company's interests. (NPR; Folkenflik et al.; 2022)

An investigation into Matrix-linked sites revealed a pattern of "staggeringly positive" coverage for Alabama Power. Outlets like APR and Yellowhammer News frequently published utility press releases verbatim under generic "STAFF" bylines. Bill Britt, editor of APR, admitted that Matrix designed the outlet's website and that his reporters were paid by the consulting firm to conduct "research," effectively blurring the line between independent journalism and paid corporate advocacy. (NPR; Folkenflik et al.; 2022)

When Public Service Commissioner Terry Dunn proposed a formal hearing to investigate Alabama Power's high electricity rates, he was targeted by a smear campaign orchestrated through Matrix-funded media. Yellowhammer News and APR published articles labeling the Republican commissioner a "loyal friend of radical leftists." The resulting negative publicity contributed to Dunn losing his 2014 re-election by 19 points, successfully preventing the rate hearing from ever taking place. (NPR; Folkenflik et al.; 2022)

In 2017, Matrix LLC hired a private investigator to surveil Tom Fanning, CEO of Alabama Power's parent company (Southern Company), and his then-girlfriend. The investigator, Derek Uman, was paid nearly $7,000 to photograph Fanning near his home and follow his partner to work. Legal filings suggest the surveillance was intended to gather leverage to influence internal corporate decisions and succession planning within the utility giant. (Al.com; Archibald, Whitmire; 2022)

Matrix founder Joe Perkins operated the firm under the mantra "Invisibility is more powerful than celebrity," emphasizing a strategy of covert influence. Following a legal fallout with former CEO Jeff Pitts, both executives traded accusations that confirmed the firm's role in manipulating public narrative through "intelligence gathering" and secret payments, though each claimed the other was responsible for the most controversial tactics. (NPR; Folkenflik et al.; 2022) & (Al.com; Archibald, Whitmire; 2022)

In 2016, the historic African-American newspaper The Birmingham Times was purchased by the "Foundation for Progress in Journalism," a non-profit funded with over $220,000 by the Alabama Power Foundation between 2014 and 2016. Although the foundation's board president was a vice president at Alabama Power, this conflict of interest was never disclosed to readers. The outlet ceased independent investigative reporting, primarily republishing utility press releases while ignoring critical issues like coal ash pollution in Alabama. (The Guardian; Green Miranda; 2024)

Through its control of local media, Alabama Power systematically suppressed negative public interest news between 2022 and 2023. Omitted topics included: three consecutive rate hikes, a forced $62 million refund for excessive profits, and health risks (mercury/arsenic) linked to coal ash landfills in Black communities like Uniontown. This "media silence" strategy allowed the utility to maintain a "good neighbor" public image while stifling debate on the actual economic and environmental costs. (The Guardian; Green Miranda; 2024)

Matrix shrewdly took advantage of the near collapse of the local newspaper industry and a concurrent plunge in trust in media to propel its clients' interests. As former Miami Herald executive editor Tom Fiedler stated: "The reduction in just the size of the press corps covering state government has created a vacuum that tends to be filled by people who have agendas beyond serving the public interest." Readers have been unknowingly immersing themselves in an echo chamber of questionable coverage for years. (NPR; Folkenflik et al.; 2022)

In 2015, Alabama Power launched the Alabama News Center, a "brand journalism" platform entirely paid for by electricity customers, as confirmed by assistant treasurer Brian George. Communications strategist Ike Pigott admitted the utility took inspiration from Chevron's "Richmond Standard", a secretly oil company-run community news site, to "bypass news organizations" and establish itself as "a source of news." While the site discloses its Alabama Power ownership on its homepage, it does not do so in stories picked up by aggregators like Google and Apple News. (The Guardian; Green Miranda; 2024)

Even before creating its own news entities, Alabama Power was aggressive in squashing negative news coverage, frequently threatening lawsuits or demanding meetings with top newsroom leaders. In 2001, Birmingham's Fox6 station killed a story about an elderly woman who died after Alabama Power shut off her electricity; a station executive who later went to work for Alabama Power spiked the piece. Two Alabama Political Reporter journalists recounted episodes in which critical articles about Alabama Power received intense and unusual editorial scrutiny, with one story never published (The Guardian; Green Miranda; 2024).

Diethelm & McKee (2009) document how the American Petroleum Institute developed a 1998 "Global Climate Science Communications Plan" to recruit "scientists who share the industry's views of climate science", replicating the Philip Morris "Whitecoats" model for secondhand smoke. Jacques et al. (2008) find that 92% of skeptical environmental literature is linked to conservative think tanks, many also active in denying tobacco harm. Supran et al. (2023, Science) explicitly cite Oreskes & Conway for the Seitz-Singer-Nierenberg trajectory from tobacco to climate denial. (Environmental Politics; Jacques et al.; 2008) & (The European Journal of Public; Diethelm, McKee, 2008) & (Science; Supran et al.; 2023)

Stover describes how deniers arbitrarily select data points, often 1998, an anomalously hot year, to simulate a warming pause. The article confirms that 17 of the last 18 years were among the hottest on record and that each decade since 1990 has been warmer than the previous one. The Heartland Institute is cited for publishing headlines such as "decade-long cooling," masking the upward trend visible over longer timescales. (Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists; Dawn Stover; 2014)

In 2007, the Heartland Institute published a list of "500 scientists whose research contradicts man-made global warming scares" (Dennis T. Avery). The list includes researchers from prestigious institutions (Columbia, Harvard-Smithsonian, Woods Hole) but promotes scientifically contested claims: that warming is caused by "natural 1,500-year cycles," that sea level is not rising rapidly, and that species face no extinction risk. Diethelm & McKee (2009) classify this tactic as "use of fake experts": individuals presented as authorities whose views are "entirely inconsistent with established knowledge," often recruited through front organizations with concealed industry ties. (The Heartland Institute; 2007) & (The European Journal of Public; Diethelm, McKee, 2008)

Jacques et al. (2008, Environmental Politics) analyze 141 skeptical environmental books (1972-2005): 92.2% are linked to conservative think tanks. Proliferation exploded after 1992, when the conservative movement replaced the "red scare" with the "green scare." The 1992 Rio Earth Summit served as a critical event: Dixie Lee Ray, former director of the Atomic Energy Commission, described environmentalism as "the next great threat to freedom" in an interview funded by the Free Congress Committee and the Competitive Enterprise Institute. 81% of skeptical books were published after 1992. Conservative think tanks function as a "counter-intelligentsia" that media present as "independent experts" to balance scientific consensus, creating the "duelling scientists" norm (Boykoff & Boykoff 2004, cited in Jacques et al.). (Environmental Politics; Jacques et al.; 2008)

Supran et al. (2023, Science) quantitatively evaluate all global warming projections documented by Exxon/ExxonMobil scientists (1977-2003): 63-83% accurately predicted subsequent warming, with an average of 0.20 ± 0.04°C/decade, identical to academic/government models (0.19 ± 0.03°C/decade). ExxonMobil correctly dismissed the prospect of a coming ice age, predicted when human-caused warming would first be detected (2000 ± 5), and reasonably estimated the "carbon budget" for <2°C (251-716 GtC, vs. current 442-651 GtC). Yet publicly, the company: (i) emphasized uncertainties (1988 strategy: "emphasize the uncertainty"); (ii) denigrated models (CEO Lee Raymond 1999: "completely unproven climate models"; Rex Tillerson 2013: "not competent"); (iii) mythologized 1970s global cooling (contradicting its own scientists); (iv) stayed silent on "stranded fossil fuel assets" in a carbon-constrained world. The disconnect between private knowledge and public communication is documented in lawsuits by dozens of U.S. cities and states. (Science; Supran et al.; 2023)

In 2024, Michael Mann won a 12-year defamation lawsuit against Mark Steyn and Rand Simberg, who had likened his paleoclimatology work to pedophilia; the jury awarded $1 million in punitive damages to Steyn and $1,000 to Simberg, ruling that "falsely attacking climate scientists is not protected speech" (Voosen, Science, 2024). In 2023, Fazackerley (The Guardian) documents how British scientists describe Twitter/X under Musk as the "Wild West": Mark Maslin (UCL) reports a "huge increase" in insults and rude comments; Sean Boyle, former Twitter sustainability lead, was fired during Musk's purge. Ed Hawkins (Reading University, 94,000 followers) sees a "huge increase" in denier accounts with conspiracy theories, many with paid subscriptions to rank higher in replies, "a coordinated effort to make climate denial appear more prevalent than it is." Richard Betts (Exeter University) reports "outright hostility increased," while Friederike Otto fears NGOs and activists no longer see tweets about bona fide scientific reports. (The Guardian; Fazackerley Anna; 2023) & (Science; 2024)

Hamilton (2012, The Conversation) analyzes the "luke-warmists": figures such as Bjørn Lomborg, Ted Nordhaus and Michael Shellenberger (Breakthrough Institute), Roger Pielke Jr., Daniel Sarewitz, Mike Hulme. These "seem to accept the results of climate science, but interpret them to make them less threatening: emphasizing uncertainties, minimizing dangers, and advocating a slow, cautious response." The Hartwell paper (2010), written by 12 conservative intellectuals (plus one woman and a representative of the Japanese Iron and Steel Federation) at an English country house funded by the Japanese steel and automobile industries, proposes addressing climate with the design principle of Lancelot "Capability" Brown's English gardens: "delivering the visitor in a relaxed and amused frame of mind." Hamilton notes this approach completely excludes the influence of fossil fuel lobbies, defending the economic status quo as "sacrosanct." The essential goal is "to silence the alarm bells rung by climate scientists." (The Conversation; Clive Hamilton; 2012)

Sparkman et al. (2022, Nature Communications, N = 6,119) identify a "false social reality" in the United States: 80-90% of Americans underestimate support for mitigation policies. While 66-80% actually support these policies (carbon tax 67%, renewables on public lands 80%, 100% renewables 66%, Green New Deal 66%), Americans estimate support at only 37-43%. Supporters outnumber opponents 2:1, but public perception is inverted. This "pluralistic ignorance" is fueled by: (i) false consensus effects (conservatives underestimate more); (ii) more conservative local norms; (iii) consumption of conservative media (Fox News, Breitbart). The perception error is ≥20% in every state and demographic group, including California and New York. State-level estimates do not differ from national ones, the distortion is "non-specific and robust." (Nature Communications; Sparkman Gregg et al.; 2022)

The disinformation campaign centers on Washington lawyer Dan Backer, who directs web design firms like Studio Psyclone to maintain and update American Action News on his behalf. The site relies on specific political writers, such as Kevin Boyd and pseudonymous authors like "Remington Strelivo," who coordinate directly with Dan Backer to produce content. (BuzzFeed News; Craig, Tarini; 2017)

The campaign uses a pioneering model leveraging hyperpartisan news to drive donations to affiliated PACs without disclosing that the website and committees share the same origin, featuring a blank "About" page and no owner list. (BuzzFeed News; Craig, Tarini; 2017)

The methodology involves aggregating articles from other media enriched with biased commentary, inserting undisclosed donation links (over 110 promotional articles, with only 11 labeled as sponsored), and featuring quotes from Backer without disclosure. (BuzzFeed News; Craig, Tarini; 2017)

The main platform is the website americanactionnews.com, operated by American Action News LLC. The network includes satellite sites: AmericanUpdate.com, TrumpTrainNews.com, GOPPresidential.com, Truedaily.news, and ICYMInews.com — the latter two sharing the same Google AdSense and Analytics codes and hosted on the exact same exclusive server as GOPPresidential.com. The site attracts an estimated 3 million unique monthly visits. Connected PACs also utilize "email list rentals" and "online advertising" as contact channels. (BuzzFeed News; Craig, Tarini; 2017)

A pro-Trump group called Great America Alliance released an ad attacking the former FBI director [James Comey]. The ad was covered by several media outlets, including a conservative news website, American Action News, which published a story headlined, “BREAKING: Pro-Trump Group ATTACKS Comey.” [...] Stop Hillary PAC... had been cited in at least 70 articles on AAN... draft broadcaster and publisher Laura Ingraham to run against Democratic Senator Tim Kaine. (BuzzFeed News; Craig, Tarini; 2017)

Beyond mainstream social media, the Internet ReseFEC records also show that AAN received just over $40,000 in revenue from four different PACs connected to Backer in 2015–16... [BuzzFeed News] connected to Backer, his company, and/or AAN via public domain registration records, IP addresses, and Google AdSense and Analytics IDs. (BuzzFeed News; Craig, Tarini; 2017)arch Agency maintained a substantial footprint on Tumblr and used American-based proxies to access Reddit and the viral meme site 9Gag during the 2016 election cycle. (Wikipedia; List of fake news troll farms) & (The Daily Beast; Ackerman et al.; 2018)

Backer is notorious in Washington for filing paperwork on behalf of a slew of PACs that popped up at the height of the tea party movement... Backer is widely acknowledged as a pioneer in creating and funding hybrid PACs, merging traditional PACs with super PACs that can raise and spend unlimited money. (BuzzFeed News; Craig, Tarini; 2017)

American Action News shares the office of Republican-affiliated political action committees. Attorney Dan Backer connects to American Action News. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation campaigns in the United States) & (open secrets; Anna Massoglia; 2020)

Clone Zone, launched in 2015, allows users to clone and edit any website simply by entering a URL (Evans, 2015). Its effectiveness was proven when a fake TechCrunch article, announcing a $1.8 million funding round, was widely believed despite visible logos, triggering genuine acquisition rumors (Evans, 2015; Thompson, 2016). The tool aims to democratize the art of spoof-making, letting users create fake spins on popular sites with as little time and effort as it takes to craft a tweet (Thompson, 2016), demonstrating that visual branding can override critical judgment. (Vice; Evans Claire L.; 2015) & (The Atlantic; Thompson Matt; 2016)

While creators Balasanov and Teachworth framed Clone Zone in 2015 as an art project to democratize satire, it has since been classified among fake news websites (Wikipedia, 2016). The tool exploits a structural vulnerability: by copying the branding of trusted outlets like the New York Times, it leverages professional aesthetics to bypass skepticism (Wired, 2016). This creates a dangerous ambiguity where artistic tools provide the exact infrastructure needed for systemic disinformation. (Wired; Reynolds Emily; 2016) & (Wikipedia; List of fake news websites)

In March 2016, a cloned New York Times article, claiming Elizabeth Warren's endorsement of Bernie Sanders, went viral on Facebook, receiving shares even from official Sanders campaign groups (Wired, 2016). The Times was forced to issue a public retraction (The Washington Post, 2016). The fake proves that Clone Zone requires no technical skills to generate real electoral impact. The disinformation strategy relies on cognitive asymmetry: the shared URL on social media (where the domain is often hidden) and the institutional layout induce readers to skip verification, exploiting a "window of credulity" before corrections emerge. ((Wired; Reynolds Emily; 2016) & (The Washington Post; Dewey Caitlin; 2016)

The creators of 4REAL defended Clone Zone as a "commentary on the culture of uncontrolled information spread" and a reflection on the very nature of the Internet (The Washington Post, 2016). However, this artistic frame serves as a conceptual shield: the tool carries no ads, yet tacitly promotes disinformation by providing a gallery of examples and nudging users toward creating viral clones (The Washington Post, 2016). The stated motivation, "democratizing satire", masks a diffusion model identical to that of trolls and conspiracy theorists: both spread disinformation, evade responsibility by retreating into the belief that online everything is permissible, and draw concrete benefit when a hoax goes viral (The Washington Post, 2016). The substantive difference is that Clone Zone, unlike commercial fake news sites, has no direct profit motive but amplifies its own visibility and that of the 4REAL studio through induced virality. (The Washington Post; Dewey Caitlin; 2016)

Clone Zone highlights that, in the age of social feeds, trust in journalism has been reduced to recognizing design and branding elements: the New York Times "T" automatically triggers confident reading (Vice, 2015). When anyone can capture a publication's layout, edit it, and share it on social media, where details are skimmed and URLs are often truncated or hidden, the intrinsic vulnerability of that trust is exposed (Vice, 2015). Balasanov observed that "a website is just a website," yet it is precisely this formal equivalence between original and clone that makes disinformation structurally possible: the average reader does not verify the full URL, and browsers increasingly hide the real address (Vice, 2015; Wired, 2016). Clone Zone's strategy is thus to exploit the "labor of truth," which requires more clicks and attention, against the ease of emotional sharing. (Vice; Evans Claire L.; 2015) & (Wired; Reynolds Emily; 2016)

After the viral spread of the fake Warren-Sanders article, the New York Times contacted 4REAL sending a cease-and-desist request, forcing the creators to remove the clone; Clone Zone will no longer include the Times in its index (The Washington Post, 2016). This reaction demonstrates that the disinformation strategy has measurable institutional impact: it is not innocent satire, but an attack on the credibility capital of traditional media. Selective removal, however, did not deactivate the tool, which remains operational for other domains, highlighting how ex post moderation is insufficient against the speed of viral propagation. (The Washington Post; Dewey Caitlin; 2016)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: Following the 2013 Gezi Park protests, the ruling AKP party recruited a paid army of approximately 6,000 social media operatives, known as "AK Trolls," to spread pro-Erdoğan propaganda and systematically attack political opponents. The operatives were instructed to use "positive political language" to correct "misinformation" about the party, though the coordinator declined to name specific individuals when asked by media. (The Guardian; Benedictus Leo; 2016)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: State-sponsored trolls utilized coordinated waves of insults to silence critics; a notable case involved journalist Emre Kizilkaya, who was repeatedly targeted with "Zionism" accusations from inauthentic profiles after criticizing the government's handling of a hostage negotiation. The attacks arrived in bursts from accounts with unconvincing profiles, making bizarrely similar accusations.  (The Guardian; Benedictus Leo; 2016)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: In 2014, the troll unit created a fake Twitter account in the name of musician Erkan Ogur to post controversial comments about state intelligence. These fabricated posts were then used as a pretext by local AKP authorities to cancel Ogur's scheduled concerts. Later, Erdoğan's daughter Sumeyye was recorded asking a party advisor for help from "our trolls." (The Guardian; Benedictus Leo; 2016)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: Twitter removed 7,340 accounts engaged in "coordinated inauthentic activity" targeting Turkish citizens. The network was identified as a centralized tool used to amplify support for President Erdoğan and the AKP while attacking opposition figures (DW.com; 2020)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: The Turkish government utilizes private PR firms, such as Bosphorus Global, to operate "fake" fact-checking platforms like FactCheckingTurkey.com. These groups masquerade as independent monitors to discredit foreign media reports and promote government narratives as absolute truths. The site does not use transparent methodology; conclusions are usually reached by referencing government statements as the sole source. (Poynter Institute; Sözeri Efe Kerem; 2017)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: Experts argue that Turkey established a "post-truth regime" by adopting the format and language of fact-checking to achieve moral superiority. These fake checkers (e.g., FactCheckingTurkey) lack transparent methodologies and rely almost exclusively on anonymous government officials as their sole "sources of truth." Andrew Moshirnia notes this represents "foreign-directed efforts to create imposter fact-checkers" that threaten the integrity of legitimate verification networks. (Utah Law Review; Moshirnia Andrew; 2020)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: Leaked emails (the "RedHack" archive) revealed that Bosphorus Global, the entity behind several fake fact-checking sites, was funded by Berat Albayrak, the former Turkish Energy Minister and son-in-law of President Erdoğan. The budget featured significant allocations for servers, firewalls, network infrastructure, and salaries for web designers and software developers. (Poynter Institute; Sözeri Efe Kerem; 2017)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: In April 2017, the Turkish government (via the BTK) blocked Wikipedia for refusing to delete articles labeling Turkey a "state sponsor of terrorism" in Syria. Although justified as a "national security" measure, the block was ruled a violation of the right to freedom of expression by the Turkish Constitutional Court on 26 December 2019, which declared the government's actions disproportionate and lacking a legal basis. The court ordered the ban lifted immediately in a 10-6 vote. (Wikipedia; Block of Wikipedia in Turkey)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: The Turkish Information and Communication Technologies Authority (BTK) systematically mandates Internet Service Providers to implement "throttling" (intentional bandwidth slowing) on X, YouTube, and Facebook during political crises. This technical manipulation obstructs the real-time sharing of media to neutralize social media as a mobilization tool while avoiding the diplomatic fallout of a total blackout. The method was documented during the 2013 Gezi Park protests, the 2016 coup attempt, and the 2022 earthquakes. (Wikipedia; Mass Media in Turkey) & (Wikipedia; Internet Censorship in Turkey)

CAMPAGNA: COUNTER CRITICISM OF TURKEY IN FOREIGN MEDIA
EVIDENZA: Unlike the U.S. where disinformation often emerges from grassroots, in Turkey "most of the fake news comes from the government. But the opposition is not exempt, especially in the case of refugees they use fake news." This top-down model makes state-sponsored fact-checking proxies particularly effective, as they can cite official sources that independent checkers cannot verify. (Politico; Zia Weise; 2018)

The original Reuters transcript confirms that Medvedev explicitly cited the movie "Men in Black" as the official source of information regarding extraterrestrials. The entire off-air context was satirical, featuring jokes about Santa Claus and Putin's punctuality, which rules out any nature of a formal "disclosure." (Reuters, 2012; Il Fatto Quotidiano, 2012)

Mikhail Gorbachev, who held the Russian nuclear briefcase for six years, officially dismissed Medvedev's statements as "total nonsense." This refutation confirms the absence of extraterrestrial dossiers within Russian state security protocols. (Il Fatto Quotidiano, 2012)

The disinformation was fueled by the "off-air" nature of the footage, which leaked via a pool signal. This leak was exploited by conspiracy actors to frame an obvious joke as a "forbidden truth" accidentally revealed, facilitating the spread of over one million deceptive links within days. (Reuters, 2012; Il Fatto Quotidiano, 2012)

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: Erin Elizabeth, founder of HealthNutNews, was identified by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) as part of the "Disinformation Dozen", a small group responsible for up to 65% of anti-vaccine content on social media. Her platform systematically weaponized the deaths of medical professionals to fuel distrust in public health institutions and promote unverified alternative treatments. (Wikipedia).

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: Disinformation outlets, primarily HealthNutNews.com and Neon Nettle, fabricated a narrative linking the deaths of various holistic and medical doctors to a supposed discovery of "cancer-causing enzymes" (Nagalase) in vaccines. Fact-checking investigations proved the deaths were entirely unrelated, ranging from verified natural causes and suicides to domestic incidents, such as the murder of Dr. Theresa Sievers, which was a murder-for-hire plot orchestrated by her husband for insurance money. (PolitiFact, 2017; Alex, Kasprak, Snopes,2018; Wikipedia).

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: The campaign utilizes the "Nagalase" enzyme and the "GcMAF" protein as pseudo-scientific anchors. While the campaign claims doctors were murdered to suppress the "truth" about these substances, major health organizations (FDA, UK Government) have warned that GcMAF is unauthorized, unproven, and potentially dangerous. Scientific journals retracted the original papers supporting these theories due to lack of evidence and procedural fraud. (PolitiFact, 2017)

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: The conspiracy relies on "circular reporting," where fringe sites like Neon Nettle cite defunct blogs like ConspiracyClub.co or TheBigRiddle.com as sources. This creates an illusion of widespread reporting for a story that has no factual basis, a tactic designed to bypass social media filters and exploit "information voids" during health crises. (PolitiFact, 2017)

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: Snopes identifies a fundamental logical fallacy used in this campaign: "cherry-picking" deaths from a population of over one million active physicians in the U.S. By isolating 60+ deaths (natural causes, accidents, or suicides) over several years and ignoring the thousands of doctors who die of common causes, disinformation agents create the statistical illusion of a "targeted purge" that does not exist. (Alex, Kasprak, Snopes,2018)

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: Investigations show that most "victims" in the list were not high-level cancer researchers but chiropractors, acupuncturists, or holistic practitioners. These individuals lacked the laboratory access or clinical background required to discover "secret enzymes" in vaccines. The narrative of a "groundbreaking discovery" is an artificial motive added by conspiracy blogs to justify the claim of assassination. (Alex, Kasprak, Snopes,2018)

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: Snopes highlights that this campaign functions as a "fear-based marketing" tool. By framing these doctors as "martyrs" silenced by "Big Pharma," fringe websites build an "us vs. them" mentality. This distrust drives audiences away from institutional medicine and toward the unregulated natural supplements sold by the very sites spreading the disinformation. (Alex, Kasprak, Snopes,2018)

CAMPAGNA: DOCTORS FOUND DEAD AFTER CANCER DISCOVERY
EVIDENZA: The campaign is classified as an "evergreen" or "zombie" hoax. Even when law enforcement confirms a death was a domestic incident (e.g., the murder-for-hire of Dr. Sievers) or a clear suicide (e.g., Dr. Bradstreet), the names are never removed from the "death list." This ensures the number of "victims" continues to grow, maintaining a high level of perceived threat for years. (Alex, Kasprak, Snopes,2018)

Chevron operates proprietary media outlets, such as the Richmond Standard in California, which are managed directly by its corporate PR firm, Singer Associates. Investigative reports show that these platforms systematically exclude negative operational data, such as a 2021 pipeline rupture leaking 800 gallons of diesel into San Francisco Bay and a 2023 refinery flaring event. In 2024, when Chevron settled a $20 million air quality penalty, the outlet omitted the words "fine" and "lawsuit," reframing a compulsory legal sanction into a voluntary initiative. (Sources: NPR/Floodlight, 2024; Nieman Lab, 2024; LA Times, 2014)

Chevron deploys a centralized PR infrastructure to insert corporate-funded media platforms into regions suffering from a collapse of independent journalism. The company targets structurally vulnerable areas like Richmond and the Permian Basin, where 20% of counties lack any local news source, to fill the information vacuum with proprietary narratives. This "newsroom-for-hire" approach allows the corporation to achieve a near-monopoly on regional civic discourse. (Sources: NPR/Floodlight, 2024; Gizmodo, 2022; The Guardian, 2022)

The campaign relies on "contextual blending," interspersing fossil fuel propaganda and misleading reports on carbon intensity with high-engagement, non-controversial local content such as high school sports and animal rescues. Given the "all-or-nothing" structure of binary options, this requirement mathematically guaranteed the loss of capital. As early as 2013, the AMF reported blocked accounts, refused refunds, and software manipulation. (Autorité des marchés financiers; Québec; 2013)

The Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission (CySEC) fined Banc De Binary €10,000 for concealing relevant information in its CIF authorization application submitted in August 2012. The sanction specifically concerned the concealment of the existence of close links between Banc De Binary and another company. The CySEC highlighted that the failure to communicate accurate information limits the regulator's oversight capacity and undermines public trust in the financial system. (LeapRate; 2014)

In 2018, the Banc De Binary fraud generated a secondary scam: Leonel Alexis Valerio Santana and Frank Gregory Cedeno, the latter employed at a fast-food restaurant in Orlando, impersonated SEC agents to extort additional funds from the original victims. From 2015 to 2017, they sent emails with fake documents and the SEC seal, promising refunds from the $11 million settlement in exchange for "fees." They targeted at least 95 victims (in Australia and the UK), requesting over $1.3 million; at least 25 victims paid over $235,000. The funds were transferred to the Dominican Republic to accomplices including Valerio's family members. (Wikipedia; Banc De Binary) & (Reuters; Raymond, Nate; 2018) & (FinanceFeeds; Saks-McLeod, Andrew; 2018)

An extensive open-source investigation by the NGO EU DisinfoLab exposed a massive pro-India international influence network operating globally since 2005. Managed by the New Delhi-based holding firm Srivastava Group, the operation weaponized over 750 fake local media outlets (such as the Times of Geneva and Manchester Times) across 116 countries. This network systematically hijacked the branding of defunct historical newspapers (dubbed "zombie websites") and registered hundreds of fraudulent, undeclared NGOs to aggressively target the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC) and the European Parliament, with the primary geopolitical objective of discrediting international perceptions of Pakistan and China. (Wikipedia; Fake news in India) & (The Hindu; Bhargava, Yuthika / EU DisinfoLab; 2019) & (BBC World Service; Carmichael, Flora & Hussain, Abid; 2019)

To manufacture unearned international legitimacy for its anti-Pakistan lobbying campaigns within the United Nations, the India-aligned Srivastava Group network committed severe global identity theft. Investigative researchers documented that the network fabricated articles under the names of non-existent foreign journalists and fraudulently registered a deceased Harvard international law professor, Louis B. Sohn, as an active participant at UN Human Rights Council sessions years after his death in 2006. Furthermore, when its primary European asset, the Brussels-based portal EP Today, was exposed and shut down by EU authorities, the network demonstrated extreme institutional resilience by immediately reincarnating the operation under a new fraudulent entity called EU Chronicle. (Wikipedia; Fake news in India) & (BBC News; Hussain, Abid & Menon, Shruti; 2020) & (Politico Europe; Saeed, Saim & Kayali, Laura; 2020) & (Dawn; Jahangir, Ramsha; 2020)

Investigative findings established that the ultimate target audience of the Srivastava Group's foreign ghost media network was not the European electorate, but the domestic public within India. The network constructed an institutional laundering loop where Asian News International (ANI), India's largest multimedia news agency, systematically picked up, repackaged, and syndicated propaganda manufactured by these fake European portals (such as EU Chronicle). ANI intentionally distorted individual, personal commentaries from obscure, far-right European politicians to present them to the Indian public as an "official, unanimous EU consensus" supporting Indian military or foreign policy, laundering these fabricated narratives into mainstream Indian television and print media to manipulate domestic public opinion. (Wikipedia; Fake news in India) & (BBC News; Hussain, Abid & Menon, Shruti; 2020) & (Politico Europe; Saeed, Saim & Kayali, Laura; 2020) & (Dawn; Jahangir, Ramsha; 2020)

During the 2019 Indian general elections, which international media and tech researchers structurally defined as "India's first WhatsApp election," the domestic disinformation architecture shifted heavily toward encrypted messaging channels. Coordinated digital investigations by VICE News and the fact-checking platform Alt News established that the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) systematically instrumentalized WhatsApp's closed, end-to-end encrypted ecosystem to bypass public journalistic scrutiny. By deploying tens of thousands of coordinated cell administrators, the political machine flooded private chat groups with unverified, highly emotional rumors engineered to inflame communal polarization, exploit religious anxieties, and spark real-world social panic among voters. (Wikipedia; Fake news in India) & (Vice; Gilbert, David; 2019) & (Alt News; Sidharth, Arjun; 2019)

During the nationwide Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA) protests, Amit Malviya, the national chief of the ruling BJP's official Information Technology (IT) Cell, was publicly documented distributing heavily manipulated, cropped, and distorted video clips across social media platforms to alter public perception of the demonstrators. In Lucknow, Malviya shared altered footage to falsely claim that local protesters shouting "Kashif saab zindabad" (praising a local leader) were chanting pro-Pakistan slogans ("Pakistan Zindabad"). Similarly, at Aligarh Muslim University, he deliberately misrepresented student political chants opposing Hindutva ideology, framing them as hate speech targeted against the entire Hindu minority community. (Wikipedia; Fake news in India) & (Scroll.in; Chaudhuri, Pooja; 2020)

In an attempt to mitigate viral falsehoods during the 2019 elections, Facebook expanded its verified fact-checking network in India by certifying regional partners — NewsMobile, India Today Group, Vishvas.news, Factly, and Fact Crescendo — under the International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) umbrella. These partners monitored content in six languages (English, Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Malayalam, Marathi). However, India has 22 official languages, and the encrypted nature of WhatsApp limited the visibility of viral content to external monitors. The initiative therefore faced structural constraints in addressing the full scale of multi-lingual, cross-platform disinformation. (Wikipedia; Fake news in India) & (Business Today; 2019)

In 2024, responding to the encyclopedic documentation of its historical role in the Srivastava Group's propaganda laundering network, Asian News International (ANI) initiated a ₹2 crore ($240,000) defamation lawsuit against the Wikimedia Foundation in the Delhi High Court. ANI legally challenged the long-standing Wikipedia article that characterized the news agency as "a propaganda tool for the incumbent central government." Independent media analysis and legal experts confirmed that the disputed encyclopedic entry was not digital vandalism, but a collaborative synthesis based strictly on public secondary sources, prior judicial findings, and verified investigative reports by independent, accredited news organizations. (Wikipedia; Asian News International vs Wikimedia Foundation) & (Scroll.in; Bhalla, Vineet; 2024) & (The Indian Express; Shah, Nishant; 2024)

During the 2024 Delhi High Court proceedings in the case CS(OS) 524/2024, the Indian judiciary applied severe coercive pressure against the structural neutrality of open-source knowledge bases. Justice Navin Chawla ordered Wikipedia to disclose the private, confidential user data of the volunteer editors who compiled the criticism section against ANI, without first establishing a prima facie case of malicious defamation. Following procedural delays by the Wikimedia Foundation, the court threatened to completely revoke Wikipedia's statutory "safe harbour" protection under Section 79 of India's IT Act, effectively exposing the platform to total domestic censorship and criminal liability, accompanied by the explicit judicial warning: "If you don’t like India, please don’t work in India." (Scroll.in; Bhalla, Vineet; 2024) & (The Indian Express; Shah, Nishant; 2024)

Local Report Inc. (Florida, 2021) operates at least 51 websites with generic names (Milwaukee Metro Times, Mecklenburg Herald, Tri-City Record) that mimic non-partisan local outlets. Target: swing states (Arizona, Colorado, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin). Schema: local/sports news interspersed with highly partisan pro-Democratic political articles. The "About Us" pages do not disclose the connection to The American Independent (TAI), a progressive organ launched by David Brock (founder of Media Matters). Six TAI authors contribute to most of the sites. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (Axios; Markay, Wheatley; October 6, 2022)

NewsGuard assigned the sites linked to TAI a score of 44.5/100 with the warning: "Proceed with caution: this website fails to maintain several basic journalistic standards." The judgment is based on the failure to separate journalistic activity from a political agenda, opaque ownership, and the systematic violation of fundamental transparency principles. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (NewsGuard; Arvanitis, Sadeghi; September 20, 2022)

Local Report articles serve as a steady stream of favorable news layout exploitable by political allies: Democratic Party of Georgia and Michigan, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Democratic Secretary of State of Michigan, Color of Change, Democratic Coalition. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (Axios; Markay, Wheatley; October 6, 2022)

On September 28, 2022, Nick Wooten of the Columbus Ledger-Enquirer accused Local Report of plagiarizing his article on Georgia's abortion ban, distorting it to insinuate that Governor Brian Kemp could order investigations. The plagiarized article received wide resonance from Stacey Abrams and the Democratic Party of Georgia; Abrams later deleted the tweet and linked to the original. Following NewsGuard's report, Meta removed several advertisements for violating advertising policies. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (Axios; Markay, Wheatley; October 6, 2022)

In September 2022, NewsGuard identified five sites launched in April 2022 — The Arizona Independent, The Michigan Independent, The Ohio Independent, The Pennsylvania Independent, and The Wisconsin Independent — which appeared to be independent state news outlets but constituted a coordinated effort to push Democratic voters in the midterm elections. The network spent approximately $39,000 on anti-Republican Facebook advertising (August–September 2022), with ads disguised as local articles. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (NewsGuard; Arvanitis, Sadeghi; 2022)

In addition to online ads, the network delivered unsolicited printed newspapers to doorsteps in Wisconsin, Michigan, and Pennsylvania. The ownership structure is opaque: American Independent Media, a 501(c)(4) incorporated in Washington DC on April 4, 2022, has a single "founder" identified as a partner of the Elias Law Group law firm (stated mission: "to help Democrats win"). It is unclear who retained the firm or the financial link to Brock's TAI. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (NewsGuard; Arvanitis, Sadeghi; September 20, 2022)

Courier Newsroom, created and funded by Acronym (a digital organization close to the Democratic Party), spent over $1.4 million on Facebook ads during the 2020 cycle to promote flattering articles about over a dozen Democratic representatives at risk of re-election. Structured as a for-profit news outlet, it is not required to disclose donors or expenditures, evading the mandatory transparency required for PACs. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (POLITICO; Thompson, Alex; 2020)

Funders of Acronym: Reid Hoffman (LinkedIn) and Laurene Powell Jobs (Emerson Collective). The seven local sections use generic names (Cardinal and Pine, Keystone, Up North News) that suggest traditional newspapers. Kelly McBride (Poynter): "It's extremely opaque to the consumer [...] the very purpose of that site's existence is different." Brendan Fischer (Campaign Legal Center): "Neither Democrats nor Republicans want to get into the business of defining what a media entity is," leaving the space open to abuse. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (POLITICO; Thompson, Alex; 2020)

According to academic estimates from 2022, there are approximately 1,200 right-wing "pink slime" sites compared to fewer than 70 on the left. The conservative prevalence is due to Brian Timpone’s Metric Media network, which operates over 1,000 local sites. In 2020, the network grew from 450 to over 1,200 sites, with over 700 activated that year. Over 90% of the articles are algorithmically generated or repurposed from legitimate sources. (Wikipedia; Pink-slime journalism) & (Columbia Journalism Review; Bengani, Priyanjana; 2020)

In 2024, ProPublica traced the Catholic Tribunes distributed in mass across Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, unaffiliated with the Catholic Church, back to the Timpone/Metric Media network, featuring content that "undermines Kamala Harris and supports Donald Trump." The newspapers mimic diocesan design to exploit religious credibility. Dioceses and parishes issued warnings to parishioners. Ben Lyons (University of Utah): "It is compromising credibility by appearing as a local news source tied to the Catholic Church." (Wikipedia; Pink-slime journalism) & (ProPublica; Richards, O'Matz; 2024)

The Snopes investigation (March 4, 2019) into Star News Digital Media, Inc. (The Tennessee Star, The Ohio Star, The Minnesota Sun) documents the political concealment mechanism that Local Report replicates on the Democratic side. Founders Michael Patrick Leahy, Steve Gill, and Christina Botteri are conservative activists linked to the Tea Party. The explicit strategy: "targeting swing states with conservative-leaning news." The sites present themselves as "impartial local newspapers" but share 237 identical entries across all three sites. (Wikipedia; List of political disinformation website campaigns) & (Snopes; Palma, Kasprak; 2019)

The network systematically conceals political conflicts of interest: "investigative reporter" Chris Butler was a pro-Bill Lee PAC spokesperson, and "senior reporter" Laura Baigert serves as treasurer for the Roving Patriots PAC. Furthermore, the founders' consulting firm (Gill Media, Inc.) illicitly received ~$32,000 from political candidate Joe Carr in exchange for 9+ favorable, undisclosed promotional articles in The Tennessee Star. Media experts from UW-Madison and Gannett condemned the infrastructure, stating that mixing hidden campaign financing with undeclared partisan advocacy fundamentally violates professional journalism standards. (Snopes; Palma, Kasprak; 2019)

An investigation by BuzzFeed News identified a network of websites and a YouTube channel (generating over 15 million views) operating under the brand "American Intelligence Media" (AIM). The network is managed by Tyla Wells and Douglas Gabriel, a couple operating Montessori schools in Michigan, who utilize the political pseudonyms "Betsy Ross" and "Thomas Pain." The platform circulated targeted conspiracy theories regarding public figures, including Mark Zuckerberg, accrediting Michael McKibben as their primary research source. McKibben is a tech entrepreneur who had previously lost a patent lawsuit against Facebook, where he claimed that Zuckerberg hacked his son's Harvard email address to steal a document outlining a plan for a social network. (BuzzFeed News; Lytvynenko, Silverman; 2019)

The AIM network published an anonymous article under the pseudonym "John," in which an alleged former Harvard roommate of Zuckerberg asserted that "Mark Zuckerberg is an impostor used by the CIA." Written in the first person, the article includes false claims regarding Zuckerberg's sexual orientation and alleges that Facebook was created under the direct orders of government intelligence agents. AIM officially stated that it had "quickly verified that many of the assertions... are true," concluding that the document was "authentic." The investigation documented that these claims systematically rehashed the exact same conspiratorial arguments previously voiced by McKibben during YouTube interviews hosted by AIM. (BuzzFeed News; Lytvynenko, Silverman; 2019)

The anonymous article targeting Zuckerberg was subsequently adopted and republished by Collective Evolution, a fringe syndication platform commanding over 5.3 million followers on Facebook, thereby extending the reach of the defamatory campaign from fringe circles to mainstream social media audiences. Furthermore, the AIM network produced a coordinated six-episode YouTube video series dedicated entirely to interviews with McKibben, systematizing the dissemination of these false institutional accusations through high-visibility visual channels. (BuzzFeed News; Lytvynenko, Silverman; 2019)

Following the publication of the "Zuckerberg Dossier," the AIM network expanded its targets by publishing an interview with an anonymous source designated as "Jane Doe," who claimed to have worked at "Google/Facebook/DARPA." This article leveled false accusations against former Google CEO and Chairman Eric Schmidt, attempting to structurally link him to the prior fabrications regarding Facebook. This expansion shifted the narrative from a localized defamation campaign against Mark Zuckerberg into a broader, interconnected conspiracy theory involving multiple major technology corporations and U.S. government defense agencies.  (BuzzFeed News; Lytvynenko, Silverman; 2019)

The first murder allegations against Marilyn Monroe emerged in 1964 from anti-communist activist Frank A. Capell's self-published pamphlet The Strange Death of Marilyn Monroe. Capell claimed Monroe's death was part of a communist conspiracy and accused Robert F. Kennedy of ordering her assassination to cover up an alleged affair. His credibility was seriously questioned because his only source was columnist Walter Winchell, who had received much of his information from Capell himself, creating a circular self-citation. (Wikipedia, Death of Marilyn Monroe)

In 1973, author Norman Mailer published Marilyn: A Biography, repeating Capell's claims without evidence and speculating that Monroe was killed by the FBI or CIA. Mailer later recanted these allegations in a 60 Minutes interview, admitting he made them to ensure commercial success for his book, and believed Monroe's death was "ten to one" an "accidental suicide". (Wikipedia, Death of Marilyn Monroe)

In 1985, investigative journalist Anthony Summers published Goddess: The Secret Lives of Marilyn Monroe, based on 650 interviews. Summers claimed that Robert F. Kennedy was involved in Monroe's death and had removed evidence from the scene. However, academic literature has criticized Summers' methodology: scholar Sarah Churchwell observed that the interviews often repeated "second- or third-hand accounts" and that Summers "proffered but did not prove" a series of sensational claims. (Wikipedia, Anthony Summers)

In 1982, Los Angeles County District Attorney John Van de Kamp conducted a "threshold investigation" into Monroe's death. After over three months of work, the investigation found no credible evidence to support murder theories and did not disagree with the original investigation's findings, though it conceded that "factual discrepancies" and "unanswered questions" remained. (Wikipedia, Death of Marilyn Monroe)

In 1982, private detective Milo Speriglio published Marilyn Monroe: Murder Cover-Up, based on statements from Lionel Grandison, a former Los Angeles County coroner's office employee. Grandison claimed to have seen Monroe's "red diary" and extensive bruising on her body. However, Grandison had been fired from the coroner's office for stealing from corpses, making him an unreliable source. The subsequent investigation found no evidence to support Speriglio's claims. (Wikipedia, Death of Marilyn Monroe)

In the 2000s, prosecutor John Miner published alleged transcripts of audio tapes Monroe had recorded before her death. Miner claimed the tapes proved Monroe could not have killed herself. However, the tapes themselves have never been found, and Miner remains the only person to claim they existed. Biographer Lois Banner challenged the authenticity of the transcripts, noting that Miner had lost his law license, lied about his work, and attempted to sell the transcripts to Vanity Fair without being able to produce them. (Wikipedia, Death of Marilyn Monroe)

Deputy coroner Thomas Noguchi performed the autopsy on August 5, 1962. Toxicological analysis concluded that the cause of death was acute barbiturate poisoning, with lethal levels of chloral hydrate and pentobarbital. No signs of external wounds or bruises were found. In his 1983 memoirs, Noguchi refuted allegations of discrepancies: he explained that stomach lining hemorrhaging indicated oral ingestion; that in addicts pills would be absorbed more rapidly; denied that Nembutal leaves dye residue; and concluded that the most probable cause of death was suicide. (Wikipedia, Death of Marilyn Monroe)

In 2018, the website Science Vibe published a hoax claiming a "dying 78-year-old CIA agent" had confessed to killing Marilyn Monroe. PolitiFact (Poynter Institute) debunked the story: the alleged agent "Normand Hodges" is a fictional character; the published photo is actually of Michael Tyrrell, a hospital prisoner (The Guardian, 2013); no credible sources exist for the alleged statements. The hoax was recycled by multiple disinformation sites. (PolitiFact/Poynter Institute; Soellner; 2018)

A study published in Sleep Medicine (Elsevier, 2013) analyzed Monroe's medical prescriptions. In her final months, she was prescribed a dozen different psychoactive drugs, mainly barbiturates, but also other hypnotics and amphetamines. Her last doctor claimed to have prescribed only pentobarbital and never chloral hydrate, a claim contradicted by toxicological results. Barbiturates had been known for decades to cause tolerance, dependence, and accidental overdose; the lack of real medical oversight and the presence of frivolous interests created the conditions for a tragic outcome. (SciDirect: Sleep Medicine; De Entrambasaguas; 2013)

CAMPAGNA: NFL TEAM REFUSES TO PARTECIPATE IN PRIDE MONTH
EVIDENZA: In June 2021, following Carl Nassib's coming out as the first active openly gay player in NFL history, the league released a nationwide broadcast spot with the message: "Football is gay. Football is lesbian. Football is beautiful. Football is queer... If you love this game, you are welcome here. Football is for everyone." This institutional positioning transformed the NFL into a focal point for political debates on corporate social advocacy. (Wikipedia; History of LGBTQ marketing) & (The Washington Examiner; Lee, Michael; 2021)

CAMPAGNA: NFL TEAM REFUSES TO PARTECIPATE IN PRIDE MONTH
EVIDENZA: Prior to Super Bowl LVI (February 2022), the NFL collaborated with advocacy organization GLAAD to host "A Night of Pride" at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles. The event featured approximately 150 players, sports executives, and media professionals. Darra Gordon, GLAAD Vice President and COO, stated: "LGBTQ athletes need to see more stories of athletes like them, who are supported by their teammates, because many of them are accepted for who they are." (Wikipedia; Homosexuality in American football) & (Los Angeles Blade; Masters; 2022)

CAMPAGNA: NFL TEAM REFUSES TO PARTECIPATE IN PRIDE MONTH
EVIDENZA: In June 2024, a digital campaign spread a fabricated headline claiming Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin had ordered his team to boycott Pride Month activities, calling it "woke nonsense." Reuters Fact Check traced the narrative to Esspots.com, a site that publishes politically inflammatory content behind a disclaimer stating all stories are "entirely fictional and created solely for entertainment purposes." The content was subsequently shared on social media without its original satirical context. (Reuters Fact Check; 2024)

CAMPAGNA: NFL TEAM REFUSES TO PARTECIPATE IN PRIDE MONTH
EVIDENZA: Reuters Fact Check directly contacted the Pittsburgh Steelers' senior director of communications, who stated via email that the news about Tomlin was inaccurate. The investigation verified that Tomlin never issued anti-LGBTQ+ statements nor ordered players to abstain from Pride Month activities. The case demonstrates how unverified content can achieve viral status on social media before authoritative correction can be disseminated. (Reuters Fact Check; 2024)

In April 2024, a social media post spread a headline claiming the NFL had "banned Taylor Swift from participating in the Super Bowl" because "she is too much of a distraction." The story was first published on Esspots.com, a satirical website with a disclaimer stating all content is "entirely fictional." NFL communications director Tim Schlittner stated via email the reports were "false." (Reuters Fact Check; NFL did not ban Taylor Swift from Super Bowl"; 2024)

In June 2024, another post claimed "the NFL lost about $700 million because of Taylor Swift, banned from next season." The story was first spread by satirical website SpaceXMania on May 11, 2024. Reuters found no credible source attesting to economic losses for the NFL linked to Swift's presence, nor any notice on the league's website banning Swift from attending games. (Reuters Fact Check; Fact Check: Taylor Swift not banned from NFL games; 2024)

In September 2024, a Facebook post claimed "Taylor Swift faces a 10-game suspension from the NFL following her controversial political involvement," referring to her endorsement of Kamala Harris. The NFL announced no such ban. Fake news sites such as SpaceX Fanclub had previously published similar invented headlines. (PolitiFact; Taylor Swift not banned from next NFL games (but maybe this zombie claim should be; 2024)

In January 2024, The New York Times reported that Biden's campaign considered Swift the "biggest and most influential endorsement target" for the 2024 election. A single Instagram post by Swift in September 2023 had generated 35,000 new voter registrations. (Wikipedia; Political impact of Taylor Swift) & (The New York Times; Epstein, Reid J. et al.; 2024)

In January 2024, far-right figures spread theories that Swift was a "secret Pentagon agent" in a psychological operation to support Biden. Vivek Ramaswamy tweeted speculations about a "presidential endorsement from an artificially culturally propped-up couple." The Pentagon rejected the claims as "conspiracy theories." (Wikipedia; Political impact of Taylor Swift) & (The New York Time; Weisman, Jonathan; 2024)

Logically (February 2024) analyzed how theories about Swift followed a "rage bait" pattern in which far-right figures transform cultural events into conspiratorial narratives. Jared Holt (Strategic Dialogue) noted these figures are "primary sources of information for modern conservatives" with "financial support from Republican elites." (Wikipedia; Political impact of Taylor Swift) & (Logically; Scott, Francesca; 2024)

A Facebook post from April 30, 2024 claimed that "the U.S. women's team will immediately resign if the Olympic Committee allows Lia Thomas to try out." PolitiFact verified the claim was a variation of a fake story from a satirical site. No credible evidence or public statements support it. (Politifact; us swimming team didn’t threaten to quit over lia t; 2024)

A Facebook post from December 14, 2024 claimed that "the men's swimming team refuses to compete against Lia Thomas, calling her a 'cheat.'" PolitiFact verified the claim originated as satire on SpaceXMania, which explicitly states: "Nothing on this page is real!" PolitiFact searched Google and the Nexis database and found no supporting evidence. (Politifact; laim that mens team refused to compete against lia; 2024)

A study of 29 transgender men and 46 transgender women in the U.S. Air Force examined the effect of gender-affirming hormones on athletic performance. After 2 years of feminizing therapy, differences in push-ups and sit-ups between transgender women and cisgender women disappeared, but transgender women were still 12% faster in running. The authors conclude that the 15-31% athletic advantage shown by transgender women before therapy declined with treatment, but after 1 year of testosterone suppression (as required by World Athletics) they still retained a 9% faster mean run speed. (British Journal of Sports Medicine / PubMed;Roberts et al.; 2020)

A review in Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews (2023) describes how testosterone concentrations are the primary determinant of sex differences in athletic performance. Policies on transgender women in sports vary drastically across federations (World Athletics, NCAA, FIFA, World Rugby), creating a fragmented landscape reflecting social values more than scientific consensus. The authors note that transgender athlete participation in elite sports is a relatively rare occurrence, but political and media attention is disproportionate. (PubMed Central, Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews, 2023)

MedicalOutline.com is an AI-generated website spreading false and potentially harmful health information, with clickbait headlines such as "Can Lemon Cure Skin Allergies?", "What Are 5 Natural Remedies for ADHD?" and "How Can Cancer Be Prevented Naturally?". The site displayed advertisements from nine major brands (including Citigroup, Subaru, GNC) served through Google. Despite Google's policies prohibiting ads on "automatically generated spam content," 90% of major brand ads on these sites come from Google Ads. (Technology Review; Tate Ryan-Mosley; 2023)

NewsGuard identified 217 AI-generated junk news sites across 13 languages, with approximately 25 new sites discovered weekly. A single site (World-Today-News.com) produced over 1,200 articles per day. These sites abuse programmatic advertising, automated ad placement systems, to generate revenue. About one-quarter of flagged sites carried programmatic ads from major brands. Of 393 major brand ads found, 356 were served by Google. The Association of National Advertisers estimates that globally approximately $13 billion is wasted annually on "made-for-advertising" sites. (Technology Review; Tate Ryan-Mosley; 2023) & (Gizmodo; kyle Barr; 2023)

NewsGuard identifies these sites by searching for error messages typical of generative AI systems, such as "As an AI language model, I am unable to provide medical advice" or "Sorry, I cannot fulfill this request as it goes against ethical and moral principles." These fragments indicate content produced without human supervision. MedicalOutline.com explicitly contained the phrase "As an AI language model, I am not able to provide medical advice" at the beginning of an article. (Technology Review; Tate Ryan-Mosley; 2023) & (Gizmodo; kyle Barr; 2023)

Google Ads, the world's largest advertising market ($168 billion in annual revenue), is responsible for 90% of major brand ads on AI-generated disinformation sites. Despite policies prohibiting ads on "automatically generated spam content," Google removed ads from Medical Outline only after journalists flagged it, and spokesperson Michael Aciman stated that AI-generated content is not "an inherent violation" of policies. (Technology Review; Tate Ryan-Mosley; 2023) & (Gizmodo; kyle Barr; 2023)

The cost of AI content generation is less than 5% of a site's total operating cost. A single site produced 8,600 articles in one week. NewsGuard discovers ~25 new AI-generated sites weekly. This makes the model economically advantageous and rapidly scalable, flooding the web with health disinformation at minimal cost. (Technology Review; Tate Ryan-Mosley; 2023) & (Gizmodo; kyle Barr; 2023)

The Association of National Advertisers estimates $13 billion is wasted annually on "made-for-advertising" sites. Brands participate in automated auctions for ad space and do not know which sites display their ads. This opacity transforms major brands into "unwitting supporters" of health disinformation, as NewsGuard's Jack Brewster states. (Technology Review; Tate Ryan-Mosley; 2023)
